query: As-cast HfMoTaTiZr has high strength at room temperature and elevated temperature but a relatively high density of 10.21 g cm−3. What single intervention could reduce its density without sacrificing its mechanical properties at room temperature and at elevated temperatures, including approximately 1000 °C? State the proposed intervention and mechanism, predict directional changes relative to as-cast HfMoTaTiZr, define the applicable temperature and loading boundaries, identify supporting prior evidence, and propose an experiment and rejection criterion that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Replacing the heavy Hf component with a lighter element – for example, substituting Hf with Sc – in the as‐cast HfMoTaTiZr alloy (yielding an alloy such as ScMoTaTiZr) will lower the density without significantly degrading its high‐temperature and room‐temperature mechanical properties.
generation.material_initial_state: An as‐cast equiatomic HfMoTaTiZr refractory high‐entropy alloy with a density of approximately 10.21 g/cm³ and excellent strength at room temperature and around 1000 °C.
generation.intervention: A single compositional change where Hf is partially or fully replaced by a lighter element (e.g., Sc) while keeping the other elements (Mo, Ta, Ti, and Zr) unchanged in near‐equiatomic proportions.
generation.conditions: Samples would be produced by conventional arc melting or vacuum arc melting and homogenized similarly to the as-cast baseline. Mechanical testing should be conducted under quasi‐static loading at room temperature and at elevated temperatures around 1000 °C (ideally in the same strain-rate regime as the baseline tests) in an inert atmosphere to minimize oxidation effects.
generation.structural_mediator: The resulting alloy is expected to maintain a single-phase BCC solid solution microstructure similar to the baseline alloy.
generation.mechanism: Sc, being significantly lighter than Hf, reduces the overall alloy density. At the same time, it can substitute into the lattice and contribute to solid-solution strengthening through size-misfit and electronic interactions. This allows retention of high strength and ductility at both room temperature and elevated temperatures (~1000 °C) typical for refractory alloys.
generation.predicted_outcome: A measurable reduction in density (potentially lowering the value below 10.21 g/cm³) while maintaining or only slightly altering the high yield and flow strength at room temperature and around 1000 °C; the phase stability and ductility should remain comparable to the original as-cast HfMoTaTiZr alloy.
generation.baseline: As-cast equiatomic HfMoTaTiZr with density 10.21 g/cm³, high strength at room temperature, and robust high-temperature performance (~1000 °C).
generation.boundary: The hypothesis applies to conditions where the alloy is used in environments ranging from room temperature up to approximately 1000 °C under quasi-static mechanical loading; tests should be performed in an inert or controlled atmosphere to avoid oxidation effects.
generation.uncertainty: The precise magnitude of the density reduction and the preservation of mechanical properties will depend on the extent of Hf replacement and the possible impact on phase stability. There is uncertainty regarding whether a full or partial substitution is optimal to maintain the balance of properties.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare samples of the proposed Sc-substituted alloy (e.g., ScMoTaTiZr) using the same casting and homogenization procedures as the baseline HfMoTaTiZr alloy. Perform microstructural characterization (XRD and SEM) to confirm that the BCC single-phase solid solution is maintained. Then, conduct mechanical tests including room-temperature and elevated-temperature (≈1000 °C) tensile or compression tests along with density measurements.
measurements: Yield strength and ultimate tensile/compressive strength at room temperature and at ≈1000 °C
Phase structure via XRD and microstructure via SEM
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the Sc-substituted alloy does not show a meaningful reduction in density (e.g., remains near 10.21 g/cm³) or if its mechanical properties degrade substantially (for instance, with a >10% lower yield or ultimate strength compared to the baseline at room temperature or at 1000 °C), or if secondary phases detrimental to high-temperature performance develop, the hypothesis will be considered falsified.

cited_evidence.text: AbstractNowadays refractory high-entropy alloys (RHEAs) are regarded as great candidates for the replacement of superalloys at high temperature. To design a RHEA, one must understand the pros and cons of every refractory element. However, the elemental effect on mechanical properties remains unclear. In this study, the subtraction method was applied on equiatomic HfMoNbTaTiZr alloys to discover the role of each element, and, thus, HfMoNbTaTiZr, HfNbTaTiZr, HfMoTaTiZr, HfMoNbTiZr, HfMoNbTaZr, and HfMoNbTaTi were fabricated and analyzed. The microstructure and mechanical properties of each alloy at the as-cast state were examined. The solid solution phase formation rule and the solution strengthening effect are also discussed. Finally, the mechanism of how Mo, Nb, Ta, Ti, and Zr affect the HfMoNbTaTiZr alloys was established after comparing the properties of these alloys.Keywords: high-entropy alloys, refractory high-entropy alloys, alloys design, elevated-temperature yield strength, solid solution strengthening effect

Accordingly, RHEAs display excellent high temperature resistance, high melting point (> 2000 °C), and higher high temperature strength, which has wide potential for applications in high temperature equipment. For examples, in 2010, the first RHEA, NbMoTaW RHEA, was fabricated by Senkov. The yield strength of NbMoTaW RHEA at 1600 °C is 405 MPa, and the working temperature limit of 1600 °C is much higher than that of nickel-based high temperature alloys about 1300 °C. In Xia’s study, the thermal stability of MoNbTaVW RHEA thin film was studied, and the experimental results show the body-centered cubic solid solution phase of MoNbTaVW RHEA is still very stable up to 1800 K. In Zhang’s experimental study, the plastic deformation mechanism of MoNbTaVW RHEA under high pressure was observed. It was found the active dislocation growth is mainly responsible for the high strength in the MoNbTaVW RHEA. In Yang’s study, they found an effective way to improve the oxidation resistance of MoNbTaVW RHEA by using Si/Al pack cementation coatings, which also improves the mechanical properties of MoNbTaVW RHEA at high temperatures. Several theoretical models of solid-solution strengthening have been proposed to explain how different constituent elements affect room-temperature or elevated-temperature strength [,]. We previously designed a RHEA that exhibited higher elevated-temperature strength and discussed the effect of the constituent elements on equiatomic HfMoNbTaTiZr alloys by using the subtraction method []. For higher room-temperature strength, one should add elements such as Mo, which significantly interact with the other elements. For higher elevated-temperature strength, one should add the elements that possess a high melting point such as Mo, Nb, or Ta. For higher ductility, one should add more Nb. With Ti or Zr addition, both the elevated-temperature strength and the density decrease.
